title: Quality Assurance Procedures for Mesoscale Meteorological Data
authors: Christopher A. Fiebrich, Cynthia R. Morgan, Alexandria G. McCombs, Peter K. Hall Jr., and Renee A. McPherson
venue: Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology, 27(10), 1565–1582
objective: Review and share general, automated, and variable-specific quality-assurance procedures used for mesoscale meteorological data.
data_and_method: Technical review of network QA practices and procedures; not a single labelled benchmark experiment.
findings: Highlights that meteorological QA must address variability in space and time and combines multiple process stages, automated checks, and human assessment.
limitations: A procedural review; its network-specific thresholds and operations should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to VILD0.
relevance: Supports treating range, temporal, spatial, calibration, and manual review as distinct QA evidence rather than equating a statistical outlier with a sensor failure.

title: Guidelines on validation procedures for meteorological data from automatic weather stations
authors: J. Estévez, P. Gavilán, and J. V. Giráldez
objective: Propose and apply quality-assurance procedures for automatic weather-station data.
data_and_method: Meteorological observations from the Agroclimatic Information Network of Andalusia; record-structure, range, time, internal consistency, persistence, and spatial-consistency procedures.
findings: The paper presents quality flags as guidance for data users and maintenance decisions; it illustrates a multi-check validation workflow.
limitations: Procedures and thresholds arise from a specific network and application context; they are not direct labels for the present station.
relevance: Provides a meteorological validation taxonomy aligned with the project’s temporal, spatial, and physical checks.

title: Toward the Standardization of Mesoscale Meteorological Networks
authors: Christopher A. Fiebrich, Kevin R. Brinson, Rezaul Mahmood, Stuart A. Foster, Megan Schargorodski, Nathan L. Edwards, Christopher A. Redmond, Jennie R. Atkins, Jeffrey A. Andresen, and Xiaomao Lin
venue: Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology, 37(11), 2033–2049
objective: Provide recommendations for harmonizing mesonet operations, including siting, sensors, maintenance, quality assurance, and data processing.
data_and_method: Best-practice synthesis for mesoscale network operations; not a labelled anomaly benchmark.
findings: Describes five broad automated QC categories: physical limits, seasonal limits, sensor intercomparison, temporal consistency, and spatial coherency; stresses site context and metadata.
limitations: Recommendations address mesonets and require adaptation to local station cadence, climate, exposure, sensors, and metadata.
relevance: Supports cautious use of neighboring stations and station provenance when evaluating spatial disagreement.

title: Challenging problems of quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) of meteorological time series data
venue: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment, 36, 1049–1062 (published online 2021)
objective: Present a staged statistical QA/QC workflow for heterogeneous meteorological and hydrological time series.
data_and_method: Workflow demonstrated on Billy Barr (Colorado) and Barro Colorado Island (Panama) station time series; covers formatting, combining series, duplicate/outlier/extreme flags, target-frequency construction, imputation, and summaries.
findings: Shows that preprocessing, QA flagging, missing-value handling, and time-frequency alignment are connected stages in post-collection quality work.
limitations: Demonstrations are two specific use cases and do not validate the current project’s classifiers or thresholds.
relevance: Motivates careful timestamp, cadence, duplicate, missing-data, and provenance handling before anomaly interpretation.

title: The Analysis and Modelling of the Quality of Information Acquired from Weather Station Sensors
authors: Marek Stawowy, Wiktor Olchowik, Adam Rosiński, and Tadeusz Dąbrowski
objective: Model uncertainty in the quality of information acquired and processed from weather-station sensors.
data_and_method: Analyses a real station structure and measurements and develops a certainty-factor hypothesis model; includes an example using two sensors.
findings: Demonstrates how their model can attribute information quality to processing elements and sensor redundancy in its example context.
limitations: The authors describe a proprietary approach and an example station; its certainty-factor model is not validated for this project and must not be copied as a score without separate justification.
relevance: Motivates explicit uncertainty and dependence-aware evidence, while reinforcing that WeatherGuard should not manufacture probabilities.
